newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Suspected Peruvian rebels broadcast in Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Suspected Peruvian rebels broadcast in Colombia.

text.p: A group of suspected Peruvian rebels briefly took over a small cable TV station in a working-class district of Bogota and threatened fresh attacks against the Peruvian government, police sources said on Friday.

The three men said they were members of the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), which grabbed international headlines when it stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Dec. 17 and held 72 hostages for the following 126 days.

In the brief cable TV broadcast, which was beamed live to about 180,000 homes in the south of the Colombian capital late on Wednesday, the MRTA trio said that some of the rebel commandos who took over the Lima embassy residence were captured alive during a brutal counter-attack by the Peruvian military on April 22.
The Peruvian authorities said all 14 MRTA rebels were killed in the operation, which succeeded in freeing all but one of the 72 hostages alive.

In comments to Colombia's leading El Tiempo newspaper, the director of the community TV programme Fidel Juez Pardo said: "A man of about 40 years old with a Peruvian accent came up to me and said he wanted to broadcast an MRTA communique to Peru's President Alberto Fujimori."

He said the three self-proclaimed rebels called on Fujimori to show the bodies of their dead companions publicly if he wished to prove that none had been captured alive and were now being held incommunicado. They also denied claims that some of the embassy residence commandos were minors.

In the course of the interview, which they forced on Juez Pardo, one of the men, clad in a green ski mask, said Hugo Avellanada had taken over the leadership of the MRTA following the death of Nestor Cerpa in the embassy residence attack.

The rebel trio said they had been in Colombia since joining the so-called America Battalion -- an international revolutionary group made up of Colombia's now-defunct M-19 guerrilla movement, Ecuador's Alfaro Vive Carajo! and Peru's MRTA.
The bid to sow the seeds of a Latin America-wide guerrilla army was short-lived when the battalion split over tactical disagreements and a series of heavy blows dealt by the Colombian military.
A police spokesman said investigators were examining a video of the interview to determine if the men were genuine MRTA members. The three fled the studio after the broadcast.
